Today, I walked past an area that not long ago was under construction. A titanic construction project, the kind that dismantles half a city, not just the typical trench for gas or electricity.

I remember passing by it when returning from university, on days I decided to walk home instead of diving into the metro tunnel.

The construction affected one end of a giant five-lane roundabout, with hellish traffic, and I would take the roundabout to the right, right in that area.

I remember the dust rising, obstructing my vision. I remember trying to navigate through ever-changing fences and signs to avoid ending up in the middle of the road, being honked at by a double-decker bus full of tourists.

I remember that feeling of discomfort, that inconvenient feeling we all get; we don’t want our world changed, even if it's for a facelift. And that very personal thought: "What the heck are they doing here?"

Well, they were building a shopping center and some shops and restaurants around it. Some of them I’ve used regularly. And today is the first time I realize that this spot corresponds to that kind of desert of dust and fine sand, where nothing rose above two meters.

It looks nice now.

I put myself in the shoes of the people who built it, those who used their imagination, creativity, and hands. Conversations filled with excitement at the project's start, heated arguments at the first difficulties, hours contemplating giving up and dismantling everything, overcoming obstacles, interests, adapting to circumstances, conceding.

And there it is, standing, with crowds passing through it every day. With its little peculiarities, its characteristics that deviate from the initial idea and make it a unique place.

I imagine the architect, or one of the workers, passing by and thinking, "Hmm... They've placed a column there... I imagined it differently."

But that’s how it is. It's no longer theirs; it's the people's. The project finishes, it’s delivered, and it’s allowed to evolve in its own way. Whether it’s good or bad depends on people and circumstances.

Like a good song. You compose it, polish the details, study it, turn it around, almost abandon it, pick it back up, and finally... you deliver it.

And it fills with people, and columns, and life.

You let it develop, grow in people's hearts, and in some cases, it doesn't succeed, and you see it die.

You create again only to eventually destroy; that’s how art is.

At first, attachment to the projects prevents you from being objective. One of those cases where you can’t see the forest for the trees. You suffer when your project is modified, adapted to specific needs, ultimately given life and made real.

But you don't want it real; you want that representation in the physical world of what you had in your mind for so long.

But if it has no life, what good is it? You have to let light in, let the wind batter it, let it get wet. Only then can you know if the project has been a success. When it becomes the people's property, that ultimate act of generosity.

They are two sides of the same coin: creating and destroying; one cannot exist without the other.

However... it has always been easier to destroy than to create. It depends on each person which side of the coin they feel comfortable with.
